stories.headline: Back to class in Calallen, with the storm plan taped by the door
stories.dek: As the school year begins across Nueces County, teachers are setting up classrooms and districts are reviewing how they would close campuses if a hurricane threatens.
body: Leticia Ramos keeps two lists on the wall beside her classroom door. One is for the first week of school: name tags, supply bins, the order her students will line up for lunch. The other, printed on yellow paper, is what she will do if a hurricane closes the building.

"The yellow one I hope I never use," said Ramos, 45, who teaches in Calallen and lives a short drive from the city's water treatment plant on the Nueces River. "But I have been doing this long enough to know August is when you write it, not September."

The school year begins this week across Nueces County, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans as classes start. Those plans govern how families are told that campuses will close, how buildings are secured and how schools decide when it is safe to reopen.

For Ramos, the hard part of past storm seasons was never the decision to close. It was the patchwork of messages that followed. "One text, one time, from one place. That's all a parent wants," she said. "Half my families find out from a cousin's post, and then they call me to ask if it's true."

She has started the year by asking every family for a working cell number and an email address, and by telling parents to sign up for district alerts the first night, not the night a storm is in the Gulf.

County emergency managers have spent the summer making a similar pitch to the wider public, holding hurricane preparedness fairs and urging residents who do not have cars to register in advance for evacuation assistance. Ramos said she repeats the advice to parents at open house whether or not they ask.
"Fill the gas tank, fill the prescriptions, know where you would go," she said. "Then go buy the glue sticks."
On Monday morning, the yellow list goes back on the wall where she can see it. The supply bins, she said, are already full.

stories.headline: Back to school: How to make sure a storm closure notice reaches you
stories.dek: Districts across Nueces County are reviewing storm closure plans as classes begin. Here is what parents should check this week.
body: Classes start across Nueces County this week, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans before the busiest stretch of hurricane season. Harborline 6 put together a checklist so a closure notice does not slip past you.

Update your contact information. Schools send closure alerts to the phone numbers and email addresses on file. If you changed numbers over the summer, tell the front office this week, not when a storm is on the map.

Opt in to text alerts. Many districts send closure messages by text as well as by phone and email. Check your district's website for how to sign up, and save the district's number in your contacts so messages are not filtered as spam.
Know your pickup plan. If schools close early ahead of a storm, decide now who will pick up your children, and make sure that person is on the school's approved pickup list.

Plan for a ride. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to register in advance for evacuation assistance. In Texas, that is the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, or STEAR. Sign up by calling 2-1-1. Registering does not commit you to anything, but it helps planners know who will need help.
Keep medicines in mind. If your child takes daily medication, ask the school nurse how it would be handled if campuses close on short notice, and keep a backup supply at home.

Follow one trusted source. Closure decisions come from the districts themselves. Harborline 6 will carry them on air, online and in our app, but check the district's own channels before acting on a forwarded post.

stories.headline: On the first day of school, a mother's bus commute shows the gaps on the map
stories.dek: For households without cars near the bay, the city bus is the plan for work, for school and, if it comes to that, for a hurricane. Advocates want more evacuation rides.
body: The morning bus is running late, and Rosa Elizondo has already done the math. If it comes soon, she can walk her youngest to the school gate and still reach her first client on time. If it doesn't, she calls ahead and apologizes, the way she has many mornings before.

Elizondo, 38, is a home health aide and a mother of three. She rents in a low-income neighborhood near the bay and does not own a car. On Monday, the first day of school for her children, her commute looked the way it looks most days: a bus, a walk, another bus, a lot of waiting. "Mi carro es el bus," she said, laughing. "My car is the bus. And the bus has its own opinions."

Her situation is not unusual. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and community advocates have spent the summer pushing for more evacuation rides for exactly those residents. The neighborhoods with the fewest cars are often the ones closest to the water.

County emergency managers held hurricane preparedness fairs this summer and urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before a storm, so planners know where to send buses. In Texas, the list is the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, which residents can join by calling 2-1-1.

Elizondo said she still has the registration card from the county's preparedness fair but has not sent it in. "I sign up my clients. I'm always signing up somebody else," she said. "Me, I think, okay, the neighbors, the church, somebody will have a car."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs meals and supplies from her church's fellowship hall in the same part of town, said that is the gap advocates worry about most. "Everybody is counting on somebody with a car, and the people with cars are the first ones to leave," Whitfield said. "We need rides that come to the people, not people who have to go find the ride."

Elizondo's two older children caught the school bus at the corner. She walked her youngest, who is 6, to the gate herself and waved until the door closed. Then she checked the bus schedule on her phone, frowned, and started walking toward the next stop.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi anchorage stays busy as crude loadings run near record pace
stories.dek: Export tankers continue to queue offshore east of Port Aransas for berths in the ship channel, which also serves the port's role as a strategic seaport for military cargo.
body: Crude tankers continue to wait at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas as loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi run at a near-record pace, according to port activity and public AIS observations reviewed by Gulfwater.

The queue is not new. Waiting at anchor for a berth has become routine for export tankers calling at the Coastal Bend. Vessels arriving from the Gulf report to the anchorage, hold for a berth window and a pilot, then transit the entrance channel between the Port Aransas jetties and proceed up the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to terminals along the channel and the Inner Harbor.

Waiting times vary with berth schedules, weather and pilot and tug availability. The structural constraint is the channel itself: a single deep-draft route serving crude terminals, refineries, bulk docks and general cargo berths.

"Corpus Christi is running like a clock right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics who tracks Gulf Coast crude flows. "The anchorage is the buffer. When everything's moving, nobody notices it."

The same channel carries military cargo. The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation. Military port movements at commercial strategic seaports are planned around commercial traffic, with berth and staging space coordinated in advance.

Hurricane season adds a variable that operators know well. When the Coast Guard tightens port conditions ahead of a tropical system, inbound traffic can be suspended, vessels at anchor commonly put to sea to ride out the weather, and oceangoing ships in port may be required to leave or to request permission to remain. The busiest weeks of the season are still ahead.
For now, the anchorage remains full and the channel open. Gulfwater will report changes in port status as the Coast Guard and the port announce them.

stories.headline: Depot keeps hiring helicopter mechanics; air station squadrons hold a steady summer pace
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot's hiring push continues while training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi keep a normal summer schedule. Plus a reminder for families: the busiest half of hurricane season is ahead.
body: If you have spent any time in base housing or on the hangar floor this summer, you have probably heard about the depot's job openings before you saw them posted. Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and word has traveled fast through spouse networks, neighborhood group chats and the commissary checkout line.

The depot, which sits on NAS Corpus Christi, is the Army's primary depot for rotary-wing maintenance, overhauling and repairing helicopters for units across the force. Its hiring this summer has focused on mechanics, and applicants are directed to federal job announcements on USAJOBS. Spouses with aviation maintenance experience may want to check whether they qualify for military spouse preference on those announcements.

Across the airfield, the training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi are on a normal summer schedule. The station completed a routine readiness inspection earlier this summer, and base services are operating normally. For families who arrived during this summer's moving season, that means training aircraft overhead from morning into the evening. Most neighbors stop noticing after the first month.

Now the reminder. Hurricane season runs through November, and the weeks ahead are traditionally the busiest. County emergency managers have held preparedness fairs this summer and are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. That applies to military families too, especially households that share one vehicle with a service member who may be on duty when a storm comes.

Navy families: make sure your information is current in the Navy Family Accountability and Assessment System, known as NFAAS. Army families and depot civilians: ask your supervisor or sponsor's unit how accountability works for your organization after an evacuation.
Keep copies of ID cards, orders, powers of attorney and insurance papers in one waterproof folder, and tell someone outside the area where it is.
Next week: building a family hurricane plan when one spouse may be at work, on duty or deployed when the call comes.

stories.headline: Aransas Pass shrimper heads into fall season with fair catches and a fuel bill that bites
stories.dek: Huy Nguyen, a second-generation bay shrimper, says the season started fair but diesel costs are eating into every trip.
body: Huy Nguyen keeps a spiral notebook in the wheelhouse of his shrimp boat. One column is what came over the side. The other is what went into the tank. He writes both down after every trip, in pencil, before he goes home.

"The notebook tells the truth even when I don't want to hear it," Nguyen, 51, said Wednesday afternoon, tied up at the harbor in Aransas Pass after a day on the bay. The deck still smelled of salt and diesel, and a few gulls waited on the pilings in case he changed his mind about the bycatch.

Bay shrimpers reported a fair start to the season earlier this summer, and Nguyen agrees: catches have been steady and the shrimp a decent size. The problem is the other column. Fuel costs are squeezing margins for boats like his, which burn diesel by the hour whether the nets come up full or not.

"Fair is fair. Fair doesn't pay for diesel," he said. Asked how far apart his two columns are, he tapped the notebook and declined to read it aloud. "Closer than my father's were. Not in the good direction."

Nguyen is a second-generation shrimper. His father worked the same water, and Nguyen still finds the grounds by the landmarks he learned as a boy: a channel marker, a line of oyster reef, the way the bottom changes color under the boat on a clear morning. At dawn, he said, the bay goes from pewter to green as the sun clears the barrier islands, and that is still the best part of the job.

With the fall bay season now under way, he is weighing every trip against the fuel it will take. Some days he stays closer to home. Some days he gambles. "You can't catch shrimp tied to the dock," he said. "You also can't buy diesel with shrimp you didn't catch."
There is one more thing he watches this time of year. "September, I look at the sky more than the nets," Nguyen said. "The bay gives you a living. The Gulf can take it back in one night."
He closed the notebook, put it back on the shelf above the wheel, and went to see about ice.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff stargazer knows the night sky over the air station by heart
stories.dek: Jaime Ortega films the stars from his backyard, and he has learned to tell a satellite from a training plane at a glance.
body: It's 9 p.m. in Flour Bluff. The heat hangs on. Jaime Ortega sets up a tripod in his backyard and points a camera at the southeast sky.
Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer. He films the night sky on most clear evenings and posts the clips online. Planets. Meteors. The International Space Station sliding across without a sound.

He also films a lot of airplanes. Flour Bluff sits next to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, where training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule. "You learn the patterns," Ortega says. "Blinking red and green, steady path, engine noise a few seconds behind. That's a plane. That's somebody's student pilot. I don't even look up anymore."
A satellite is different, he explains. No blinking. No sound. A steady glide that fades out as it slips into Earth's shadow.

He keeps a notebook next to the tripod. Time, direction, what he thinks each light was. When he isn't sure, he writes "unknown" and leaves it there. "The sky is full of things people get excited about," he says. "Most of them are airplanes. I'd rather say 'I don't know' than say something that isn't true."
His favorite nights come after a front pushes through and the air clears over the Laguna Madre. This summer, he says, has given him plenty.

Neighbors have started wandering over when they see the tripod. Kids ask about Saturn. Retirees ask about the base. Ortega answers both the same way: look up, be patient, and don't make anything bigger than it is.
"It's free," he says, adjusting the focus. "And it's the only quiet place in town."

stories.headline: How an Army aviation brigade gets from Central Texas to a ship in Corpus Christi
stories.dek: A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer. Here is how a port movement like that generally works.
body: On most mornings, the Port of Corpus Christi is about oil. Tankers ride low in the ship channel, and more wait offshore. But from time to time, the port's cargo docks fill with something else: rows of tan Army vehicles and helicopters with their rotor blades folded back, wrapped against the salt air and waiting for a ship.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation, Army officials have said. They have not released dates, and the Army typically does not describe unit movements in detail before they happen, for security reasons. This explainer describes how such movements generally work, not the specifics of this one.

A move like this starts at the home post. Units inventory and prepare their equipment, then send it toward the seaport by rail and by highway convoy. At the port, vehicles and aircraft are staged on the docks, inspected, cleaned and prepared for the voyage. Helicopters are typically readied for sea transport with blades folded or removed and protective wrapping applied, because salt spray is hard on aircraft.
Most of the equipment then rolls aboard a sealift ship, often a roll-on, roll-off vessel built to carry vehicles. Soldiers usually travel separately and meet their equipment at the other end.

The Port of Corpus Christi is one of a small number of commercial ports designated as strategic seaports, which means it commits to making berths and staging space available for military deployments. That role shares a single ship channel with one of the busiest crude export operations in the country, where tankers routinely wait at the offshore anchorage for a berth. Military movements are scheduled around that traffic.

Weather is a factor in any port movement, especially now. The Atlantic hurricane season peaks in September, and port operations of every kind can pause when the Coast Guard restricts the channel ahead of a storm.

For residents, the signs of a movement in general are easy to spot: military vehicles on the highways, convoys near the port and aircraft on the docks. Fort Hood's public affairs office is expected to share details when it decides they can be released, and Coastline Public Radio will report them then.

stories.headline: Opinion: If you would need a ride out, ask for it now, not when the cone is on TV
stories.dek: Column: The state's evacuation assistance registry only works if the people who need it sign up before a storm has a name.
body: I have covered two hurricanes for this newspaper. The images that stay with me are not the wind or the water. They are the people on porches with a suitcase and a phone, waiting for a ride that nobody had planned for.

This summer, county emergency managers held preparedness fairs and urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance. Advocates have pushed for more evacuation rides, because bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay. Those are not slogans. They are the plain facts of where people live and how they get around, and they point to a simple request.

If you would need a ride out, register now. The State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry lets residents who need help evacuating, whether because they have no vehicle, a disability or a medical need, tell local planners in advance. You can sign up by calling 2-1-1. It is free. It does not guarantee anything, and it does not obligate you to leave. What it does is put your address on the list planners use to decide where buses go.

If you have a car, find out who on your street does not. Ask the older man two doors down whether he has somewhere to go. Ask the family with three kids and one bus pass. Offer a seat now, so the offer is already made when it matters.
If you employ home health aides, cooks, cleaners or anyone else who rides the bus to your door, ask them what their plan is. Many of them spend storm season making sure other people get out.

I am suspicious of anyone who claims to know how many people will need a ride in the next storm. Nobody knows. That is the point of the registry: to replace guesses with names and addresses, before the decisions have to be made in a hurry.

The busiest weeks of hurricane season are ahead of us. Make the call in August, while the Gulf is calm and the line at 2-1-1 is short. It is the least dramatic thing you will do all season, and it may be the most useful.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay brisk as August winds down
stories.dek: Export tankers continue to queue at the offshore anchorage as the Coastal Bend's crude gateway runs near a record pace, analysts say.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi stayed brisk through the third week of August, keeping export tankers queued at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, analysts said.

The port has loaded crude tankers at a near-record pace this summer, reinforcing its position as the largest U.S. crude export gateway. Tankers calling at the Coastal Bend now routinely spend time at anchor before a berth opens.

"The pipes are full and the docks are busy," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "As long as Corpus keeps loading at this pace, the anchorage is where you see the strain, not the price."
Holloway said traders would watch two variables into September: freight availability for long-haul voyages, and the Atlantic hurricane season, which historically peaks in early to mid-September.

"A Gulf storm doesn't have to hit Corpus to slow it down," she said. "It only has to get close enough that the Coast Guard starts changing port conditions. Then the queue offshore gets longer, and everyone downstream starts making phone calls."
Holloway said buyers read the anchorage like a gauge. "Count the ships waiting and you know how hard the terminals are working," she said. "Right now the gauge says full."

For now, the anchorage is doing its job. Tankers arrive, wait their turn for a berth and a pilot, load and sail, and the next ship in line moves up. Holloway said the routine looked unremarkable from the outside, which was the point. "Nobody writes about a queue that keeps moving," she said.
Tanker-tracking firms will tally August loadings as the month winds down, and Sabal Energy Wire will report the totals when available.

stories.headline: Forecasters expect a busy rest of hurricane season
stories.dek: An updated seasonal outlook calls for above-normal Atlantic activity through the end of the season. The Coastal Bend's peak weeks are still ahead.
body: The Gulf off Mustang Island was flat and warm as bathwater on Tuesday morning, the kind of late-August calm that makes it easy to forget what the season is for. Forecasters would like you to remember.

An updated seasonal outlook released Tuesday calls for above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season. The outlook does not predict where storms will go or whether any will reach Texas. It describes how busy the basin as a whole is likely to be.

"An outlook is a weather forecast for the whole ocean, not for your street," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "It tells us the dice are loaded a little more than usual. It doesn't tell us where they land."

The Atlantic season runs June 1 through Nov. 30, and its busiest stretch historically runs from mid-August into October, peaking in early to mid-September. Warm water is the fuel. By late summer, the Gulf has had months to heat up, and the shallow shelf off the Texas coast holds that heat well.

Arceneaux said nobody on the Coastal Bend should change plans because of an outlook. "What I want people to hear is, make sure you have a plan at all," he said. "Know your evacuation zone. Know where you'd go. Know how you'd get there. If the answer to that last one is 'I don't know,' fix that now."

County emergency managers have been sending the same message all summer, holding preparedness fairs and urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance through the state registry by calling 2-1-1.

The quiet weeks are also the time to check insurance. Homeowners policies generally do not cover flooding, and a new flood insurance policy usually takes 30 days to take effect, so a policy bought when a storm is in the Gulf may not help with that storm.

The tide gauge on Corpus Christi Bay showed nothing unusual Tuesday, just the gentle rise and fall of a summer bay. That is what an outlook cannot see, and why forecasters keep saying the same thing: prepare in the calm.

stories.headline: Busy season ahead: Build your hurricane kit before the shelves empty
stories.dek: Forecasters expect above-normal activity for the rest of the Atlantic season. Here is a kit list and the sign-ups to do this week.
body: Forecasters are calling for an above-normal rest of the Atlantic hurricane season. That does not mean a storm is coming here. It does mean now is the time to get ready, while the stores are calm and the shelves are full.
Water and food. Plan on at least one gallon of water per person per day for several days, plus food that does not need cooking. Do not forget a manual can opener.
Medicine and documents. Get a refill on prescriptions if you can. Put copies of IDs, insurance policies and medical records in a waterproof bag, and take photos of them on your phone.
Power. Flashlights, batteries, phone chargers and a battery or crank radio. If you use a generator, never run it indoors or in a garage.
Pets. Food, water, a leash or carrier, and vaccination records. Many shelters ask about pets, so plan ahead.
Know your zone. Look up whether your address is in a hurricane evacuation zone on your county emergency management website. If you are in one, decide now where you would go.

Sign up if you will need help. County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before a storm. Call 2-1-1 to join the state registry. It takes a few minutes.
Check your coverage. Flood damage is usually not covered by homeowners insurance, and new flood policies generally have a waiting period before they take effect.

Harborline 6 Weather will track every system in the Gulf this season. Download our app and turn on alerts, and always check the National Weather Service before sharing a forecast you saw on social media.

stories.headline: Your family hurricane plan, built for the season's busiest stretch
stories.dek: Forecasters expect an above-normal rest of the season. Here is a plan built for military families, including what to do if your service member is at work when a storm comes.
body: Every military family on the Coastal Bend has some version of the same story. The storm is coming, the kids need packing, the dog needs his pills, and the service member is at work, on duty or a thousand miles away. This week's column is for the person who ends up doing it alone.

Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season, and the weeks from now into October are historically the busiest. That makes this the right week to finish your plan, not the week a storm has a name.

Plan for one adult. Assume the adult at home will handle an evacuation alone, because service members and many depot employees may have duties before and after a storm. Write the plan down so a teenager or a neighbor could follow it.

Get accounted for. Navy families should confirm their contact information in the Navy Family Accountability and Assessment System, NFAAS. Army families and depot civilians should ask their unit or supervisor how accountability works for them. After a storm, commands need to know you are safe, and they will look in those systems first.

Build the folder. ID cards, orders, powers of attorney, insurance policies, vehicle titles, medical records and a list of medications go in one waterproof folder. Take photos of everything and store them where you can reach them from any phone.

Know where you would go. Find out whether your home is in an evacuation zone. Pick a destination inland and a second choice. If your command issues evacuation guidance for families, follow it, and keep receipts for travel and lodging.

Short on cars? County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1. That includes households that share one vehicle with a service member who may be at work when the order comes.
Talk to the kids. Tell them the plan in plain words. Children handle a plan better than a surprise.
Base services are operating normally. We will share official guidance from public affairs offices as soon as it is released.

stories.headline: The pastor with the list: who has no car, who has no phone, who needs a hand
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs meals and supplies from her church fellowship hall near the bay. Before every hurricane season, she updates a list that no agency keeps.
body: The list lives in a three-ring binder on a folding table in the fellowship hall, between the coffee urn and a stack of donated diapers. Pastor Gloria Whitfield keeps it in pencil. The list started years ago in a spiral notebook she carried in her purse; this summer she copied it into the binder.
"People move. People pass. People get a car and lose a car," said Whitfield, 59. "Pen is for people who think things stay the same."

The binder holds the names and addresses of neighbors who have no car, no working phone, or both. Some pages have notes in the margin: can't do stairs, needs oxygen, won't leave without the dog. Whitfield started it, she said, because nobody else in the neighborhood had one.

Her neighborhood sits near the bay, and it is the kind of place where her list is long. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates have pushed this summer for more evacuation rides for residents who cannot drive themselves out. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to register with the state's evacuation assistance registry by calling 2-1-1, so planners know where to send buses.

Whitfield supports the registry and helps people sign up, sometimes at that same folding table, on her own phone. She also knows what a registry cannot do. "A registry is a list in somebody's computer. Mine is a list with a face on it," she said. "I know which man can't climb the bus steps without help. I know which grandmother won't leave without her grandbabies' birth certificates and won't find them without me."

Relief agencies have spent the summer stocking warehouses ahead of peak hurricane season. Whitfield's warehouse is a storage closet behind the kitchen: cases of water, canned beans, baby formula, batteries. "When the big trucks come, they go to the big parking lots," she said. "We're the little parking lot. Somebody has to be."

What advocates describe as a transit gap is, in practice, a question of time. A family with a car can leave when the order comes. A family without one has to find a ride, wait for it and be ready when it arrives, often with children, medicines and pets. The longer that chain, the more likely someone is still at home when the weather turns.
Whitfield closed the binder and slid it back under the table. "Nobody should have to be brave because they're poor," she said. "That's the whole sermon."

stories.headline: At the jetties, a bait shop owner reads the summer by the line at his counter
stories.dek: Port Aransas businesses report a strong summer. Bill Hargrove, who has sold bait near the jetties for years and ridden out two hurricanes on the island, says he is grateful, and watching the Gulf.
body: Bill Hargrove can tell you how the summer went without opening his register. He points at the floor in front of his counter, where the linoleum has worn pale in a strip that runs toward the door.
"That's where the line goes," he said. "This year it went out the door and turned left."

Hargrove, 64, owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle, a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties. Port Aransas businesses are reporting a strong summer, with bait shops and fishing charters especially busy, and Hargrove said his shop was no exception. Weekend mornings, the live shrimp tank emptied early. Weekday afternoons brought families who had never held a rod and wanted to know what to buy.
"Tourists ask me where the fish are," he said. "I tell them, 'In the water. Next question.'"

He has watched the channel traffic from that corner for years: dolphins working the pass, charter boats heading out before dawn, and tankers sliding past so close to the jetties that customers stop talking to watch them go by. He knows which end of the jetties fishes best on an incoming tide and which tourists will be back for more bait in an hour.

Hargrove has ridden out two hurricanes on the island and does not recommend it. "The first time I thought I was brave," he said. "The second time I knew better." He keeps plywood cut to size and labeled by window in the back of the shop, a habit he picked up after the second one.

Forecasters said this week they expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season. Hargrove heard it on the radio between customers. "Above normal," he repeated, and shook his head. "Around here, normal is plenty."
Asked how much business was up this year, he would not put a number on it. "More than last year, less than I'd like," he said. "Same answer I've given for a long time."

Labor Day is two weekends away, and with it the end of the summer crowds. After that, Hargrove said, the island gets quiet, the locals get the jetties back, and everybody starts watching the Gulf a little more closely. "Then it's just us and the weather," he said. "And the weather doesn't buy bait."

stories.headline: North Beach packs in the late-summer crowds as one longtime resident keeps watch from his porch
stories.dek: Heat, crowds and a reminder to conserve water as summer winds down on North Beach.
body: North Beach is packed. Saturday afternoon. Umbrellas in rows. Kids in the shallow surf. Cars circling for parking in the shadow of the old aircraft carrier.

Marcus Bell watches it all from a lawn chair on his porch a few blocks from the water. He is 67, a retired welder, and he has lived on North Beach long enough to stop counting summers. "Summer people come and go," Bell says. "The wind stays."

Heavy tourism has filled the beaches on the barrier islands and along the bay all summer. With the heat hanging on, the city keeps urging residents to conserve water. Bell nods toward a neighbor's lawn sprinkler ticking away at three in the afternoon. "City says save water," he says. "That fella hasn't heard."

He notices things. The way the tide sits higher on some evenings. The way the wind swings around before a front. The way the gulls go quiet. "You live on a strip of sand between two bays and a ship channel, you learn to look," he says.

Forecasters expect a busy rest of the hurricane season. Bell keeps his plan short. "I've got water. I've got a radio. I've got a ladder," he says. Asked what the ladder is for, he just raises an eyebrow.

If you are heading to the beach this weekend: bring water, take breaks in the shade and watch for flags on the lifeguard stands. At home, the city asks residents to water lawns early in the morning or late in the evening and to fix leaky faucets and sprinklers.
The crowds will thin after Labor Day. Bell says he will still be on the porch.

stories.headline: Cones, watches and warnings: how to read a hurricane forecast before you need to
stories.dek: With forecasters expecting a busy rest of the season, here is what the forecast products mean, and why storm surge matters most on the coast.
body: The cone is the most famous graphic of hurricane season and the most misunderstood. With forecasters expecting an above-normal rest of the season, now is a good time to learn to read it before it matters.

The cone shows the probable track of a storm's center. It is drawn from the size of past forecast errors, so it widens farther out in time, and the center stays inside it roughly two-thirds of the time. It does not show how big the storm is. Wind, rain and surge routinely reach far outside the cone's edges.

"People look at the skinny line in the middle and decide they're safe if it's pointed somewhere else," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Ignore the line. Watch the whole cone, and then look past it."

Watches and warnings are the next step. A hurricane watch means hurricane conditions are possible in an area, and it is usually issued about 48 hours before tropical-storm-force winds are expected. A hurricane warning means those conditions are expected, typically about 36 hours ahead. The time between those products is when most preparation and evacuation happens, and it goes quickly.

On the coast, the number that matters most is storm surge: water pushed ashore by a storm's winds, measured in feet above normally dry ground. Surge is the deadliest part of most hurricanes, and the weather service issues separate surge watches and warnings for it.
"Wind you can hide from in a sturdy building," Arceneaux said. "Water you can't. If you're in a surge zone and you're told to leave, leave."

Surge also stacks on top of the tide. On the Coastal Bend, the shape of the bays matters: water driven into Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay has fewer places to go than water on an open beach. A storm that arrives at high tide brings that water higher still.

County emergency managers have spent the summer urging residents to learn their evacuation zones and asking those without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. Arceneaux said the best time to look up your zone is a quiet Sunday. "Do it now," he said, "while the only thing on the map is the coastline."

stories.headline: Relief warehouses fill up and freight forwarders sign standby deals as peak season nears
stories.dek: Relief agencies have stocked up ahead of the busiest weeks of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby contracts to move supplies quickly if a storm hits.
body: The supply chain for a hurricane starts months before the storm, in warehouses most people never see and in contracts most people never read.

Relief agencies have stocked their warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season, and freight forwarders have signed standby relief contracts, arrangements that let agencies call up trucks, containers and cargo space quickly if a storm strikes the region. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season, which makes those arrangements more than paperwork this year.

A standby contract works like a reservation with the terms already agreed. The forwarder commits to have capacity available, and the agency agrees in advance on rates and how to activate it. The point is to avoid negotiating prices and schedules in the middle of an emergency, when every truck and every container is in demand at once.

It helps to think of relief supplies in three layers. The first is what families keep at home: water, food, medicine and batteries for several days. The second is what neighborhood hubs, churches and local agencies keep nearby. The third is what moves in by truck and by ship after a storm, from warehouses that may be hundreds of miles away. The third layer is the largest and also the slowest, because it depends on roads, bridges and, for sea freight, an open ship channel.

The Port of Corpus Christi can be part of that third layer, receiving containers by sea. But a storm that threatens the Coastal Bend can also close the channel, and ships carrying relief cargo would wait offshore with everyone else until it reopens.

At the second layer, the stockpiles are smaller and closer to home. Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs meals and supplies from her church's fellowship hall near the bay, and she has spent the summer filling a storage closet with water, canned goods and batteries.
"The big warehouses are for the region. My closet is for the block," Whitfield said. "Both of them need to be full before the wind starts."
For households, the lesson of the layers is simple: outside help takes time to arrive. Emergency managers recommend keeping enough supplies at home to get through several days on your own.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports hit monthly high, cementing the port's outsized share
stories.dek: Analysts say the Coastal Bend gateway now handles about half of U.S. crude exports, concentrating a large share of the trade in a single ship channel.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August, analysts said Tuesday, underscoring the port's outsized role in moving U.S. crude to overseas buyers.

The port now accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts who track Gulf Coast flows, extending a summer in which tankers were loaded at a near-record pace and routinely waited at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for a berth.

"Half of the country's crude exports through one channel is a remarkable concentration," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "It's efficient right up until something interrupts it."

Holloway said the August figure reflected steady pipeline deliveries to the coast and a well-oiled routine at the terminals and the anchorage. "Nothing dramatic happened in August, and that's the story," she said. "The system just ran full."

The concentration also shapes how the market reads risk. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, and September is historically its peak. A storm that prompts the Coast Guard to restrict or close the Corpus Christi Ship Channel would pause loadings at the country's largest crude export gateway.

"September is the month this market watches the Gulf more than the price screen," Holloway said. "Nobody is predicting anything. But when one port carries this much of the load, the weather map becomes a trading tool."
Sabal Energy Wire will continue to track loadings and anchorage activity at Corpus Christi through the peak of the season.

stories.headline: Half the nation's crude exports, one ship channel: what the port's monthly high means here
stories.dek: Crude exports through the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August. The port now handles about half of U.S. crude exports, nearly all of it moving through a single channel past downtown.
body: Here is the simplest way to understand the Port of Corpus Christi's August: about half of the crude oil the United States sells abroad now leaves through one ship channel that runs past downtown Corpus Christi.

Crude exports from the port hit a monthly high in August, analysts said Tuesday. The milestone caps a summer in which the port loaded tankers at a near-record pace and tankers routinely waited at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas for their turn at a berth.

The chain behind that number is straightforward. Crude arrives by pipeline from West Texas oil fields to tank farms and terminals along the ship channel and the Inner Harbor. Tankers arrive from the Gulf, wait at the anchorage, take on a pilot, transit the entrance channel at Port Aransas and tie up to load. Then they sail. Each link depends on the one before it, and nearly all of them depend on the channel being open.
Locally, that chain supports work for terminal crews, pilots, tug operators, line handlers, truckers and the businesses that serve them. When the channel is busy, the paychecks are steady.

"Corpus got to half the market by being very good at one thing in one place," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The pipes, the tanks and the docks all grew up around that channel."

The flip side of concentration is exposure. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic hurricane activity for the rest of the season, and the Coast Guard can restrict or close the channel when a storm approaches, leaving tankers at anchor and loadings paused until it reopens.

The channel also serves the port's role as a designated strategic seaport. A Fort Hood aviation brigade is scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation, sharing the same waterway with the crude trade.

None of that is a forecast. It is a reminder of what rides on one narrow ribbon of dredged water. For most of the year, that channel is the city's economic engine. For a few weeks each fall, it is also the thing everyone watches when a storm is in the Gulf.

stories.headline: September is here: Labor Day weekend plans, and the peak of hurricane season
stories.dek: A long weekend for many families is a good time to rest, travel safely and finish the hurricane plan. Plus: squadrons wrap a steady summer, and the depot keeps hiring.
body: Happy September from all of us at Anchor & Rotor. For many families, this week means a long weekend, the first real routine of the school year and maybe one last trip to the beach. On the Coastal Bend, it also means the statistical peak of hurricane season.

Labor Day weekend first. Commands typically hold safety briefs before long weekends, and the advice never changes because it never stops being true: plan your drive, rest before you go, never drink and drive, wear a life jacket on the water and watch the kids in the surf. Expect heavy traffic to the islands and longer waits for the ferry.

On the airfield, NAS Corpus Christi's training squadrons wrapped a summer on a normal schedule, and the station completed a routine readiness inspection earlier in the season. Base services continue to operate normally. Across the field, Corpus Christi Army Depot is still hiring helicopter mechanics. If you know someone with the skills, point them to the federal job announcements.

Now the season. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of hurricane season, and the weeks just ahead are traditionally the busiest. If you built your family plan with us last week, use the long weekend to finish it. If you did not, here is the short version.

Know your zone and your destination. Fill prescriptions. Keep the gas tank at least half full. Put IDs, orders and insurance papers in one waterproof folder. Update NFAAS if you are a Navy family, or check your unit's accountability process if you are Army or a depot civilian. If your household shares one car with a service member who could be at work when a storm comes, register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1.

For families who arrived on new orders this summer: this is your first Coastal Bend hurricane season. Ask a neighbor who has been through one. They will have opinions, and most of them will be useful.
Enjoy the weekend. We will be back next week, and sooner if public affairs offices release guidance families need.

stories.headline: Need medical help to evacuate? Register before a storm, health workers urge
stories.dek: Residents who depend on oxygen, dialysis, home health visits or a ride should sign up with the state's evacuation assistance registry now. A home health aide explains why.
body: Rosa Elizondo knows which of her clients use oxygen at night, which ones cannot manage stairs and which ones keep their pill bottles in a shoebox by the bed. That knowledge is part of the job. In hurricane season, it is also a worry.

"If a storm comes, my clients can't just get in a car," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rides city buses between appointments. "Some of them can't get out of bed by themselves. Ay, you think I'm going to carry them to the bus?"

Residents without cars should sign up for evacuation assistance before a storm, county emergency managers have said. Residents with medical needs should do the same. The State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, known as STEAR, lets people tell local planners in advance that they will need help leaving, including help with mobility, oxygen or other medical equipment.
Here is what health workers recommend doing now, before any storm is on the map:
Register. Call 2-1-1 or sign up online for STEAR. Describe the help you need: wheelchair, oxygen, a service animal, someone to help you onto a bus.
Talk to your providers. Ask your doctor, dialysis center or home health agency what their storm plan is and how appointments or treatments would be rescheduled.
Stock your medicines. Keep extra prescriptions on hand if your insurance and pharmacist allow it, and carry a written list of every medication and dose.
Plan for power. If you rely on powered equipment, keep backup batteries charged and know where you would go if the power stays out.
Caregivers, plan for yourselves too. The people who look after others often leave their own plans for last.

That last one hits home for Elizondo. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, including hers, and she has helped several clients register with the state. She has not yet registered her own family.
"I keep saying I'll do mine," she said, laughing at herself. "This week. Lo prometo."

stories.headline: Labor Day getaway: expect heavy traffic to the islands and long lines at the ferry
stories.dek: Holiday crowds are heading for Mustang and Padre islands. Here is how to make the trip easier and safer.
body: It's Friday afternoon. The holiday weekend is on. Traffic is building on the JFK Causeway toward Padre Island and on the roads to Port Aransas.
Port Aransas businesses have reported a strong summer, and the last long weekend of the season usually brings one more rush. Bait shops and charters are busy. Beaches will be crowded.

Taking the ferry? Waits at the Port Aransas ferry landing in Aransas Pass can run long on holiday weekends. If you are coming from Corpus Christi, consider driving over the JFK Causeway and up Mustang Island on State Highway 361 instead.
Driving on the beach? Keep it slow. Watch for kids, dogs and people walking from their cars to the water. Park above the high-tide line.
Heat is still a factor. Carry more water than you think you need. Take breaks in the shade. Never leave a child or pet in a parked car. The city is still asking residents to conserve water at home.
In the water: swim near a lifeguard stand, check the flags and keep an eye on kids at all times. If you get caught in a current, swim parallel to shore until you are out of it.

Check the forecast before you go. Forecasters expect a busy rest of the hurricane season, and conditions in the Gulf can change over a long weekend. Harborline 6 Weather will update the forecast every morning through Monday.
Heading home Monday? Leave early or late. Midafternoon is when the causeway and the ferry line are usually at their worst.

stories.headline: Tropical Storm Rafael forms in the Caribbean; early forecasts point toward Texas
stories.dek: It is too early to say where Rafael will come ashore, forecasters say, but early tracks show a west-northwest path toward the Texas coast. Coastal Bend residents should review their plans this weekend.
body: Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean Sea on Saturday, and early forecasts show it moving west-northwest across the Yucatan Peninsula and into the Gulf, with Texas among the possible targets, according to the National Weather Service.

The sky over Corpus Christi Bay was a hard, cloudless blue Saturday morning. Sailboats rode their moorings off the marina, joggers worked the seawall, and holiday traffic was already building toward the islands. Nothing about the view suggested a storm. That is what makes the first days of a tropical system tricky.

"This is the time to pay attention, not the time to panic," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Early tracks have Texas in the picture. They also carry a lot of uncertainty. The cone is wide for a reason."

That uncertainty is normal this early. As the Ledger explained last weekend, the forecast cone shows the probable path of a storm's center, and it is widest for the days furthest out. Track forecasts tend to tighten as a storm organizes and as reconnaissance aircraft and weather balloons feed more data into the models. Intensity forecasts, how strong a storm will get, are harder still.
Rafael arrives in the heart of a season that forecasters said last month would be busier than normal. The water it is crossing is late-summer warm, the kind that gives a storm room to grow.

Many residents and visitors are on the islands for the Labor Day weekend. Arceneaux said there was no reason to cancel plans yet, but every reason to pay attention. "Enjoy the weekend, and check the forecast twice a day," he said. "If you're in an evacuation zone, spend ten minutes today thinking about what you'd do if this comes our way."

What to do now: review your family's plan, check your hurricane kit, refill prescriptions, and look up whether your home is in an evacuation zone. If you do not have a car and would need help leaving, county emergency managers urge you to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1.
No watches or warnings were in effect for the Coastal Bend as of Saturday morning. The Ledger will update this story as forecasts change.

stories.headline: Rafael forms: what it means for your Labor Day weekend
stories.dek: Tropical Storm Rafael is in the Caribbean, and early forecasts point toward Texas. No watches or warnings are in effect for the Coastal Bend. Here is what to do this weekend.
body: Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Saturday. Early forecasts show it crossing the Yucatan into the Gulf, with Texas a possible target.

What we know: Rafael is a tropical storm. Its early track points toward the Texas coast. It is too early to say where it will make landfall or how strong it will be. As of Saturday afternoon, the Coastal Bend is not under any watch or warning.

Your holiday weekend: Port Aransas businesses had a strong summer, and the beaches are busy for Labor Day. Plans can go ahead for now. Check the forecast morning and evening, keep your phone charged and know how you would get off the island if you needed to.
Do these things now, while it is easy:
Fill up the gas tank, and keep it at least half full from here on.
Refill prescriptions you will need over the next two weeks.
Get some cash. Card readers do not work without power.
Check your kit: water, food, flashlights, batteries, chargers.
Look up your evacuation zone on your county emergency management website.
No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to sign up before a storm, not during one.

A word about what you see online: forecast maps shared on social media sometimes show a single computer model run, which can swing wildly from one update to the next. Rely on the National Weather Service and your county emergency managers.
Harborline 6 Weather will update Rafael's forecast through the weekend on air, online and in our app.

stories.headline: Traders eye Tropical Storm Rafael's track toward Texas as Corpus Christi loadings run high
stories.dek: Early forecasts show a west-northwest path. Analysts say the port's share of U.S. crude exports makes any Gulf disruption a market event.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude market participants turned their attention Saturday to Tropical Storm Rafael, which formed in the northwestern Caribbean with early forecasts showing it crossing the Yucatan Peninsula into the Gulf on a track that could reach Texas.

The timing is sensitive for the U.S. export trade. Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi hit a monthly high in August, and the port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts said, leaving the market exposed to any disruption on the Coastal Bend. Tankers have been loading at a near-record pace and waiting at the offshore anchorage for berths.

"It's a long way from a tropical storm in the Caribbean to a closed channel," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "But with this much of the export market running through one port, people don't wait for the closure to start asking questions."

Holloway said traders and shipowners would watch for any change in Coast Guard port conditions at Corpus Christi, which would signal restrictions on vessel traffic. She said loading schedules for the coming week were the first thing likely to be revisited if the track held.
"Nobody reroutes a cargo on a Saturday forecast," she said. "They make a list of what they'd do, and they wait for Tuesday's."

She said the bigger question for the market was not whether loadings would pause, but for how long. A short closure ahead of a storm is routine for Gulf ports, she said. What traders price is the time it takes after a storm to inspect the channel, clear the anchorage queue and get berth schedules back to normal.

With the U.S. Labor Day holiday on Monday, Holloway said the first full read on market sentiment would likely come midweek. Sabal Energy Wire will track Rafael's path and any port status changes through the weekend.

stories.headline: On a holiday weekend in Port Aransas, the forecast becomes small talk
stories.dek: The beaches are full and the bait shops busy, but Tropical Storm Rafael is the topic at every counter on Mustang Island.
body: At Hargrove Bait & Tackle on Saturday afternoon, the conversation at the counter ran in the same order every time: shrimp, ice, how the fish were biting at the jetties, and what that storm was doing.

"Everybody's a meteorologist on Labor Day weekend," said Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns the shop a short walk from the Port Aransas jetties. "I tell them what my daddy told me. Watch the birds and watch the TV, and believe the TV."

Tropical Storm Rafael formed Saturday in the northwestern Caribbean, and early forecasts show it crossing the Yucatan and heading toward Texas. No watches or warnings were in effect for the Coastal Bend as of Sunday morning, and forecasters said it was too early to know where the storm would go.

On the island, the holiday went ahead. Port Aransas businesses have had a strong summer, and the long weekend brought one more wave of visitors: families dragging coolers across the sand, charter boats heading out at first light, a line of cars waiting at the ferry landing across the water in Aransas Pass. On the beach, a few people checked weather apps between swims. Most did not.

Hargrove said the storm talk was friendly so far. Regulars asked whether he was putting up plywood. He was not. "I cut my plywood in May. It's labeled. It doesn't go up for a Saturday tropical storm," he said. "It goes up when the man on TV stops smiling."
Asked how busy the weekend had been, he would not guess at a number. "Busy enough that I ran out of ice twice," he said. "That's my weather report."

He did take one step. Behind the counter, next to the tide chart, he had taped up a printed list of phone numbers: the county, the city, a cousin inland. "I'm not saying I'm going anywhere," he said. "I'm saying I know who I'd call."

Emergency managers urge island residents and visitors alike to know their route off the island and to check the forecast before heading home Monday. Hargrove put it more simply as he rang up a bag of frozen squid. "Have a good time," he told the customer. "And keep an eye on that thing."

stories.headline: With a storm in the Caribbean, a church starts working its list
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield began calling neighbors without cars this weekend, days before anyone knows where Tropical Storm Rafael will go.
body: On Sunday afternoon, after the last service let out, Pastor Gloria Whitfield sat down at the folding table in her church's fellowship hall, opened the three-ring binder and started at the top of the list.

Whitfield, 59, keeps a penciled list of neighbors who have no car, no working phone, or both. Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Saturday, and early forecasts show it heading west-northwest across the Yucatan Peninsula, with Texas a possible target. Nobody knows yet whether it will come anywhere near Corpus Christi. Whitfield decided not to wait to find out.
"If it turns, wonderful," she said. "Then I had a nice visit on the phone with a lot of people I love."

Her questions are the same for every call. Do you have two weeks of medicine? Is there someone who can drive you if you have to leave? Have you called 2-1-1 to register for an evacuation ride? Is your phone charged, and do you have a way to charge it if the power goes out?

The calls are her answer to a problem advocates have raised all summer. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and advocates have pushed for more evacuation rides. The county's answer has been the state's evacuation assistance registry: residents without cars are urged to sign up so planners know where to send buses.

The reason to start early is time. A household with a car can decide to leave in an afternoon. A household without one has to find out about a ride, get on a list, pack for children and pets and medicines, and be ready when a bus or a neighbor arrives. Every step takes longer, and every step depends on someone else.

One of the afternoon's calls went to Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who does not own a car. She laughed when she heard who it was. "Pastora, I know, I know," Elizondo said. "This week. For real this time."
Whitfield made a small mark next to the name and moved down the page. By early evening she had reached most of a column. She said she would finish the rest Monday, holiday or not.
"The storm doesn't know who has a car," she said. "But we do."

stories.headline: Tanker operators track Rafael as Corpus Christi anchorage holds steady
stories.dek: The ship channel remains open with tankers queued offshore. A look at what port status changes would mean for vessels at anchor and alongside if Rafael's track holds toward Texas.
body: Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Saturday, with early forecasts showing a west-northwest track over the Yucatan Peninsula and into the Gulf toward Texas. As of Monday, the Corpus Christi Ship Channel remained open, and crude tankers continued to wait at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas.

The traffic picture is the one Gulfwater has described all summer. Corpus Christi crude exports hit a monthly high in August, and the port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts. The anchorage has functioned as the buffer between arrivals and berth availability.

A tropical system changes that calculation in stages. The Coast Guard sets port conditions based on when gale-force winds are expected to arrive. As conditions tighten, inbound traffic can be suspended and the channel can be closed to all vessel movements. Vessels at anchor commonly weigh anchor and put to sea to ride out heavy weather away from the coast, where they have room to maneuver. Oceangoing vessels already in port may be required to depart before the closure or to request permission to remain.

Vessels remaining in port during a storm typically do so under conditions set by the captain of the port, which can cover mooring arrangements, crewing and readiness to get under way. Those decisions are made vessel by vessel.

Operators also plan for the other side of a storm. When a channel reopens, the queue that formed offshore during the closure arrives at once, and berth windows, pilots and tugs become the constraint. A closure of a few days can produce a backlog that takes longer than the closure itself to clear.

For now, those are contingencies. Forecast uncertainty for Rafael remains large several days out, and no change in port status had been announced for Corpus Christi as of Monday. Pilot operations and terminal loadings were continuing.
Gulfwater will report Coast Guard port condition changes for Corpus Christi and the anchorage count as they are announced.

stories.headline: Holiday crowds head home from the islands with one eye on Rafael
stories.dek: The causeway is busy, the ferry line long and the storm still far to the south in the Caribbean. Forecasters say keep watching.
body: It's Labor Day afternoon. Coolers are packed. Sunburns are settling in. Cars stack up at the ferry landing, and traffic inches across the JFK Causeway toward the mainland.

Tropical Storm Rafael is still in the Caribbean, far to the south. Early forecasts show a west-northwest track toward Texas. There is still no watch or warning for the Coastal Bend as of Monday afternoon.

At a gas station on Padre Island, a man in a fishing shirt tops off his tank and scrolls a weather app while the pump runs. Two kids in the back seat argue over a bag of chips. Nobody looks worried. A few people look curious.
Port Aransas businesses had a strong summer, and the holiday weekend brought one last rush to the islands. Now the visitors head home. For people who live here, the question is what comes next.
If you live on the Coastal Bend, this is your week to get ready, while stores are calm:
Fill your gas tank.
Refill prescriptions.
Check your kit for water, food, flashlights and batteries.
Look up your evacuation zone.
No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help. County emergency managers want that list built before any order, not after.
Heading home from the islands tonight? Be patient on the causeway, and do not drive tired. Pull over if you need a break, and keep the radio on for weather updates.
Staying on the islands this week? Know your route back to the mainland, and keep an eye on the forecast. Conditions in the Gulf can change faster than holiday traffic clears.
Harborline 6 Weather will have the latest on Rafael's track tonight at 10 and first thing tomorrow morning.

stories.headline: Tropical moisture ahead of Rafael soaks the Coastal Bend; Nueces River rising at Calallen
stories.dek: Saturated ground means more runoff with every downpour. Forecasters say the soaking is a preview, not the main event.
body: The first downpour arrived before dawn Tuesday, a gray curtain dragged in off the Gulf. Rain hammered the bayfront for a few minutes, the palms bent, and then the sun came out over wet streets as if nothing had happened. An hour later, the next one came through.

A plume of tropical moisture ahead of Tropical Storm Rafael and a stalled front soaked the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, and the Nueces River was rising at Calallen, according to the National Weather Service. Soils across the region are saturated.

"When the ground is already full, rain has nowhere to go but the streets and the rivers," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "This rain is a preview. The storm itself hasn't even reached the Gulf yet."

Saturated soil changes how a region responds to rain. Dry ground absorbs a downpour. Wet ground sends most of it straight into ditches, storm drains and creeks, which feed the river. The Nueces River gauge at Calallen, upstream of Nueces Bay and near the city's water treatment plant, is one of the readings forecasters watch most closely in a wet week, because it shows how much water is moving toward the coast.

Rafael itself remains a tropical storm in the northwestern Caribbean, with forecasts continuing to show it crossing the Yucatan and heading toward Texas. Arceneaux said moisture arriving this far ahead of a storm is a reminder that a tropical system's effects arrive in pieces, not all at once.
"People wait for the storm to show up on their street," he said. "It shows up in pieces. Rain first, then wind, then water. Use the rain days to get ready for the rest."

What to do: Never drive through water over the road; turn around instead. Clear leaves and trash from storm drains near your home if you can do it safely. Move vehicles out of low spots that pond in heavy rain. And keep finishing your hurricane plan.
River readings for the Nueces at Calallen are posted online by the weather service and updated through the day. The Ledger will update river and storm information as forecasters release it.

stories.headline: In Calallen, a teacher watches the river and the school pickup line
stories.dek: Tropical moisture ahead of Rafael is soaking the area, and the Nueces River is rising. Leticia Ramos is keeping neighbors and families in the loop.
body: Rain drums on umbrellas in the school pickup line in Calallen. Leticia Ramos stands under the awning with a clipboard and a whistle, waving cars forward one at a time.
Tropical moisture streaming ahead of Rafael and a stalled front are soaking the Coastal Bend. The Nueces River is rising at Calallen. The ground is saturated.

Ramos, 45, teaches in Calallen and lives near the river. She has started a group text with her neighbors. Twice a day, she checks the river gauge online and sends the reading. "No drama. Just what it says," she says. "People like having one person who checks, instead of twenty people guessing."

What she wants is more than a number. "A number on a website isn't a plan," Ramos says. "I want somebody official to tell us what the river means for us. Is it a little high? Is it a problem? Is it a 'move your car' problem?"
A parent rolls down a window to ask whether school will close. Ramos shakes her head. Classes are on. She points to the district alert sign-up flyer taped to the door.

If you live near the river: check the National Weather Service river gauge page for the Nueces at Calallen. Do not drive through water over the road. Move cars out of low spots. Keep your phone charged.
Rafael itself is still far to the south. Forecasts continue to show a west-northwest track toward Texas. Harborline 6 Weather is tracking it.
The last car pulls away. Ramos checks her phone. The group text has twelve new messages. She starts reading.

stories.headline: Why a soaked Coastal Bend matters before Rafael's center ever arrives
stories.dek: Tropical moisture and a stalled front have saturated soils and pushed the Nueces River up at Calallen. Here is how wet ground, a rising river and the bay can work together, and who lives closest to the risk.
body: On a street near the bay Tuesday afternoon, a storm drain gurgled and gave up. Water spread across the gutter and into a front yard that had not dried out since the morning downpour. A boy in rain boots stood at the edge of it, deciding whether it was deep enough to be worth it.

Tropical moisture pumped north ahead of Tropical Storm Rafael ran into a stalled front and soaked the Coastal Bend on Tuesday. Soils across the region are saturated, and the Nueces River is rising at Calallen. Rafael itself has not yet reached the Gulf; forecasts show it crossing the Yucatan Peninsula on a west-northwest track toward Texas.

That combination matters before the storm's center gets anywhere close. When soil is dry, it absorbs a large share of the rain that falls on it. When it is saturated, almost all new rain runs off into streets, ditches and creeks, and from there into the river and the bays.

"Rain on saturated ground is like pouring water into a full glass," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "It doesn't matter how gently you pour. It's going over the side."

Hydrologists call the next part compound flooding. Rivers drain to the coast. If a storm then pushes seawater into the bays, the river water has fewer places to go, and low-lying land near the water can flood from two directions at once: rain and river from behind, surge from the front. Which way it plays out depends on the storm's track, strength and timing, none of which is known yet for Rafael.

The geography of that risk is not evenly shared. The neighborhoods nearest the bay include many of the region's lowest-income households, and bus service and transit gaps leave many of those households without cars. Advocates have pushed all summer for more evacuation rides. Wet weeks are a reminder of why: the people with the shortest distance to the water often have the longest path to leaving.

What to watch: the weather service posts readings for the Nueces River gauge at Calallen online throughout the day, along with river forecasts when they are issued. Track and intensity forecasts for Rafael will tighten over the coming days.
What to do: keep storm drains clear where it is safe, move cars out of low spots, avoid driving through water, and if you do not have a car, register for evacuation help through 2-1-1 now.

stories.headline: Rafael becomes a hurricane; forecasters warn of rapid strengthening over warm Gulf water
stories.dek: Hurricane Rafael is gaining strength in the Gulf. No watches are in effect yet for the Coastal Bend, but forecasters urge residents to finish preparations now.
body: Rafael crossed the Yucatan Peninsula and became a hurricane over warm water in the southern Gulf, the National Weather Service said, and forecasters are warning that it could strengthen rapidly.

Rapid strengthening has a specific meaning to forecasters: an increase in a storm's sustained winds of at least 35 mph within 24 hours. It happens when a storm finds the right mix of warm water, moist air and light winds aloft, and it is one of the hardest things in weather to forecast precisely.

"Warm water is fuel, and Rafael is sitting on a lot of it," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "What worries me about rapid strengthening is that it shrinks the time people think they have. Do the things you'd do in three days, today."

The track forecast continues to show Rafael moving on a west-northwest path toward Texas. The cone remains wide enough that forecasters will not yet say where the storm will come ashore, and no watches or warnings were in effect for the Coastal Bend as of Wednesday morning.

The region is not starting dry. Tropical moisture and a stalled front soaked the Coastal Bend on Tuesday, the Nueces River rose at Calallen and soils are saturated, as the Ledger reported. Any additional heavy rain will run off quickly.

On the bayfront at sunrise, the water was a little choppier than it has been, and a long, slow swell was rolling in from the southeast. The air had the heavy, salt-sticky feel that old-timers on the coast recognize. None of that is a forecast. It is a reminder that the Gulf is busy.

What to do now: finish your kit. Refill prescriptions. Fill gas tanks. Get cash. Bring in or tie down patio furniture. Find out whether you live in an evacuation zone and where you would go. If you do not have a car, call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help. If you care for someone who needs medical help to leave, make that call today.
The weather service issues full advisories on Rafael every six hours, with updates in between. The Ledger will update this story as forecasts change.

stories.headline: Rafael is a hurricane now. Here is what military families should do this week
stories.dek: Use the quiet days to get ready, watch your command's official channels for guidance, and keep unit details off social media.
body: Hurricane Rafael is in the Gulf, and forecasters warn it could strengthen rapidly over warm water. We do not know yet where it will go. We do know that the families who handle storms best are the ones who were ready before anyone asked them to be.
If you followed our family plan columns over the last few weeks, this is the week you use them. If you did not, start here.
Finish the folder. IDs, orders, powers of attorney, insurance, medical records and a list of medications, all in one waterproof folder, with photos on your phone.
Fill up. Gas tanks, prescriptions and cash. Card readers and pumps do not work without power.
Update your contact information. Navy families, check NFAAS today. Army families and depot civilians, confirm how your unit or supervisor will reach you.
Make the one-adult plan. Service members and many depot employees may have duties before and after a storm. Plan as if the adult at home will do the evacuation alone.
Need a ride? County emergency managers urge residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. That includes families who share one car with a service member.
Watch official channels. Guidance for families will come from your command and from installation public affairs offices. We will publish it here as soon as it is released.

Keep it off social media. If you hear about aircraft schedules, unit plans or who is going where, please do not post it. Let public affairs release what can be released. That protects your service member and your neighbors.
Talk with your kids. Give them one job each. Kids handle a plan better than a surprise.
Base services continue to operate normally as of this morning. Check your command's channels before you head to any facility in the days ahead.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael: six things to do before any watch is issued
stories.dek: Rafael became a hurricane, and forecasters warn it could strengthen quickly. No watches are in effect for the Coastal Bend yet. Use the time.
body: Rafael is now a hurricane. Forecasters warn it could strengthen rapidly over warm Gulf water. As of Wednesday afternoon, nothing is posted for the Coastal Bend: no watch, no warning. That gives you time. Here is how to use it.
1. Know your zone. Look up your address on your county emergency management website. If you are in a hurricane evacuation zone, decide now where you would go and how you would get there.

2. Register for a ride if you need one. County emergency managers urge residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before any order. Call 2-1-1. If you care for someone with medical needs, register them too.
3. Fill prescriptions. Aim for at least a two-week supply. Make a written list of every medication and dose.
4. Fill the tank and get cash. Lines at gas stations grow fast once a watch is issued, and card readers do not work without power.

5. Secure your yard. Bring in or tie down patio furniture, grills, trash cans and anything else wind can throw. Clear storm drains near your home if it is safe. The ground is already saturated from Tuesday's downpours.
6. Charge everything. Phones, power banks, flashlights and radios. Download the Harborline 6 app and turn on alerts.
What not to do: do not share forecast maps from unknown accounts, and do not wait for a watch to start getting ready. Once a watch is issued, stores and gas stations get crowded fast.
Harborline 6 Weather will have Rafael's latest track tonight and every morning this week.

stories.headline: Rafael's forecast cone now covers Corpus Christi; no watch yet, but forecasters say prepare now
stories.dek: No watches are in effect yet. Forecasters urge residents to finish preparations and be ready to act if evacuation orders come.
body: The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael now covers Corpus Christi, the National Weather Service said Thursday, though no hurricane watch has been issued yet for the Coastal Bend.

A watch, when one is issued, means hurricane conditions are possible in the area. It is typically the step before a warning, which means those conditions are expected. The time between the two is when most preparation and evacuation decisions are made.

"Don't wait for a watch. This is the point where you stop planning and start doing," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "If you live in a surge zone, decide today where you'll go and how you'll get there. If you're told to leave, leave."

Rafael became a hurricane over warm Gulf water earlier this week, and forecasters have warned that it could strengthen rapidly. Arceneaux urged residents not to fix on the storm's current category. "Category tells you about wind at the center," he said. "It doesn't tell you about surge, and it doesn't tell you what the storm will be when it gets here."
