The ground is already soaked. A moisture plume and a stalled front drenched the region Tuesday, the Nueces River rose at Calallen and soils remain saturated, so heavy rain from Rafael would run off quickly into streets and waterways.
The relief supply chain is also moving. Relief shipments are being booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, as the Ledger reports today in Business.
What to do now:
Finish preparations today. Secure outdoor items, fill prescriptions and gas tanks, and charge phones and power banks.
Know your zone. If you are in a hurricane evacuation zone, pick your destination and route now.
Register if you need a ride. County emergency managers urge residents without cars to call 2-1-1.
Check on neighbors, especially older residents and people who live alone.
Follow official sources: the National Weather Service, Nueces County emergency management and your city. The Ledger will update this story through the day.

stories.headline: Rafael's cone covers Corpus Christi: what Nueces County says to do now
stories.dek: No watches are up yet, but Corpus Christi is in Rafael's forecast cone. County emergency managers say know your zone and register for a ride if you will need one.
body: The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael now covers Corpus Christi. No watches are in effect yet for the Coastal Bend.
What comes next: a hurricane watch would mean hurricane conditions are possible here. A warning would mean they are expected. Use the time before either one.
No evacuation order has been issued in Nueces County as of Thursday morning. County emergency managers say now is the time to plan for one.

"If you'd need a ride out, today is the day to call," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Call 2-1-1, give them your address and tell them who's in the house, including pets and anybody with medical needs. That's how we know where to send a bus."

Pruitt said shelter plans are ready. "If an evacuation order comes, shelters will be inland, and we will announce locations before anyone is asked to go," he said. "Don't show up somewhere because you saw it on a post. Wait for us to tell you."
Many households near the bay do not have cars, and bus service gaps make leaving harder. If that is you, register now.
Your checklist today:
Look up your evacuation zone on the county emergency management website.
Pack a go-bag for each person: medicine, IDs, chargers, clothes, snacks.
Fill prescriptions and gas tanks. Get cash.
Plan for pets: carrier, food, leash, records.
Secure outdoor items.
Where to get updates: Nueces County emergency management, the National Weather Service and Harborline 6. We will post every county announcement in our app as it happens.

stories.headline: Relief cargo booked ahead of Rafael, including 40 containers on the cargo ship Gulf Provider
stories.dek: Relief shipments are being lined up as Rafael's forecast cone covers Corpus Christi. A freight forwarder says weather and the ship channel will set the schedule.
body: The relief supply chain started moving before the first evacuation order. Relief shipments are being booked ahead of Hurricane Rafael, including 40 containers on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, according to Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder handling the booking.

"We've got 40 boxes booked on Gulf Provider, and we're working the inland legs now," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics. "The whole game is pre-positioning. You want the cargo committed and the trucking lined up so that when the port says go, you go."

As the Ledger reported last month, relief agencies stocked warehouses this summer and freight forwarders signed standby relief contracts ahead of peak hurricane season. Those arrangements set terms and capacity in advance, so that cargo can be booked quickly when a storm threatens, without negotiating rates in the middle of an emergency.
Akins would not describe what is in the containers. "Relief cargo. The agencies will tell you what's in the boxes," he said. "My job is getting them here."

The schedule depends on the storm and on the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. A ship carrying relief containers needs the same open channel and the same berths as the tankers that load crude here. If the Coast Guard closes the channel ahead of Rafael, inbound ships wait offshore until it reopens.
"Weather sets the schedule. We just hold the bookings," Akins said. "If the channel shuts, she waits like everybody else. Then we work the queue."

The forty-container figure is the one confirmed Thursday. Akins did not say whether other forwarders had booked additional relief cargo, and the agencies that own the shipments have not released details.

For the region's families, the reminder from the Ledger's August reporting still holds: outside relief is the slowest layer of the supply chain. Rafael's forecast cone now covers Corpus Christi. Emergency managers recommend having enough water, food and medicine at home to get through several days on your own.

stories.headline: With Corpus Christi in Rafael's cone, a mother without a car makes the call she kept putting off
stories.dek: Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide with three children and no car, registered for an evacuation ride Thursday. County officials say others like her should do the same now.
body: Rosa Elizondo made the call from her kitchen table between clients, the phone on speaker and her youngest doing a worksheet beside her.

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay and does not own a car, had been meaning to register for an evacuation ride since the county's hurricane fair in July. "Every week I said, next week," she said. "Then the TV put Corpus in the cone, and I said, okay, Rosa, ya."

Corpus Christi sits inside Rafael's forecast cone, though forecasters have not yet posted a hurricane watch. No evacuation order has been issued in Nueces County. But for households without cars, the time to plan is now, county officials said.

Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay. Advocates spent the summer pushing for more evacuation rides, and county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for help through the state registry by calling 2-1-1.

"If you don't have a way out, we need to know before the order, not after," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We plan the buses off that list."

The call took a few minutes. The operator asked for her address, the names and ages of the people in the household and whether anyone needed medical help. Elizondo answered, spelled her street name twice and hung up.
"Now I wait," she said. "I'm waiting for a phone call and a hurricane. Which one comes first, I don't know."

Her children have each been assigned a bag. Clothes for three days, a toothbrush, a phone charger for the ones old enough to have phones, and one toy for the youngest, who has already chosen a stuffed dog. Elizondo's bag holds the family's documents, her medicines and a folder of client phone numbers.

That folder is her other worry. Several of her clients cannot leave on their own, and she has spent the week making sure they are registered too. "They're like my grandparents," she said. "If I go, I need to know they're going."
She looked at the bags lined up by the door and shook her head. "I've packed for my clients a hundred times," she said. "First time I've packed for us."

stories.headline: Navy flies training aircraft from Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth; Army depot secures helicopters
stories.dek: NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are moving training aircraft out of Rafael's path, and Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work to secure helicopters in its hangars.
body: The engines started early in Flour Bluff on Friday. Neighbors used to the rhythm of training flights noticed the difference: aircraft climbing out and turning north, one after another, and not coming back around.

NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael, Navy officials said Friday. Corpus Christi Army Depot, which sits on the air station, has halted work and is securing helicopters in its hangars.

"Moving the aircraft is a precaution. It's what we plan and train for every season," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "Our people and our aircraft will be out of harm's way, and we'll bring them home as soon as it's safe."

The reasoning is straightforward. Aircraft parked in the open are vulnerable to high winds and flying debris, and hangar space on any base is limited. Flying them inland, to a base well outside the storm's reach, protects them and lets training resume faster once the coast is clear. Navy air stations in Texas flew aircraft inland ahead of Hurricane Harvey in 2017 for the same reason.

Navy officials did not say how many aircraft were moved or which units were involved. Coastline Public Radio does not report those details, or the movements of personnel, unless the Navy releases them.

At the depot, the Army's primary facility for overhauling and repairing helicopters, workers spent their last shifts before the storm securing aircraft and shops. Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot, said the workforce did the job and went home.

"Our workforce did what they always do. They secured the aircraft, they secured the shops, and now they're going home to take care of their families," Kowalczyk said. "We'll tell them when it's time to come back."

The forecast cone has covered Corpus Christi since Thursday, though no hurricane watch had been issued as of Friday morning. Hale said base residents and families should follow guidance from their commands and county emergency management.

For the neighborhoods around the air station, the quiet will be noticeable. Training flights are as much a part of daily life in Flour Bluff as the wind off the Laguna Madre. When they stop, people know something is coming.

stories.headline: Special edition: Aircraft head to Fort Worth. A families' guide to the days ahead
stories.dek: With training aircraft moving out and the depot securing helicopters, here is what families should know and do now. Follow your command and county officials for any evacuation guidance.
body: If you heard aircraft lifting off early this morning and wondered why, here is the answer. Training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are headed to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth to get out of Hurricane Rafael's way. Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars.
No hurricane watch has been issued yet, but the forecast cone covers Corpus Christi. That is why this special edition is coming out before our regular weekly issue.

"Families should follow their command's guidance and any county evacuation orders," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "The most important thing you can do today is make sure your command can reach you. Navy families, check your information in NFAAS."

For depot employees and their families, the message is similar. "Take care of your families first," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "Keep your phone on, and watch for word from your supervisor about when to come back."
Your checklist for today:
Account for yourself. Update NFAAS if you are a Navy family. Army families and depot civilians, confirm your contact information with your unit or supervisor.
Grab the folder. IDs, orders, powers of attorney, insurance and medical records in one waterproof bag, with photos on your phone.
Fill up and cash out. Gas, prescriptions and cash, today.
Know your zone. If you live off base in a county evacuation zone, county orders apply to you like everyone else. Plan your destination now.
Need a ride? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help.
Pets, kids, chargers. Everyone gets a bag. Every bag gets a charger.

A note on the aircraft move: if your service member is part of it, expect limited contact for a while, and please do not post details about schedules or locations. Public affairs will share what can be shared, and we will publish it here.
We will update this guide as installation public affairs offices release new information.

stories.headline: Army depot halts work and secures helicopters as Rafael approaches; workers told to prepare their families
stories.dek: One of the region's largest employers has paused production ahead of the storm. The Navy is also flying training aircraft from Corpus Christi and Kingsville to Fort Worth.
body: Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work Friday and secured helicopters in its hangars ahead of Hurricane Rafael, pausing one of the region's largest employers as Rafael's forecast track points toward the Coastal Bend.

The depot, which occupies part of NAS Corpus Christi, is the Army's primary facility for overhauling and repairing helicopters. Its hangars and shops are filled with aircraft in various stages of repair, along with the tools and parts needed to finish them. Securing that work means more than closing doors: aircraft are moved inside, components are stowed, and shops are buttoned up against wind and water.

"Our employees have done this before, and they did it well," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "When we're ready to bring people back, they'll hear it from us first. Until then, their job is their families."
Kowalczyk would not speculate on how long work would be paused. That will depend on the storm and on what crews find when they return.

The pause comes at the end of a summer in which the depot was hiring helicopter mechanics, a reminder of how much of the local economy runs through the air station's gates. Depot paychecks support households across Flour Bluff, the Southside and beyond, and the businesses that depend on them.

On the other side of the airfield, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth, Navy officials said. Moving aircraft inland protects them from wind and flying debris and frees crews to prepare the bases themselves.
The moves come a day after Rafael's forecast cone shifted to cover Corpus Christi, and forecasters have warned the storm could strengthen rapidly over warm Gulf water.

For depot employees, the practical advice is the same as for everyone else in the region: know your evacuation zone, keep your phone charged and follow county guidance. Residents without cars can register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1.

stories.headline: Plywood, gas lines and planes overhead: Corpus Christi gets ready for Rafael
stories.dek: Hardware stores are busy and training aircraft are heading north as Rafael nears. Here is where things stand Friday evening.
body: The plywood goes fast. By midday, the parking lot at a Southside hardware store is full. Carts roll out stacked with sheets, sandbags, tarps and water.
At the gas stations, lines spill into the street. People top off tanks and fill red cans. Nobody honks. Everybody checks a phone.

Overhead, training aircraft head north. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying them to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. At Corpus Christi Army Depot, work has stopped and the helicopters are locked down in hangars.

Marcus Bell, 67, carries a case of batteries and two jugs of water to the register. He has lived on North Beach for decades. "I've done this more times than these kids have had birthdays," he says, nodding at the teenagers stocking shelves. "Buy the batteries before you need the batteries. That's the whole secret."
No hurricane watch is up yet. The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael covers Corpus Christi.
What you need to know tonight:
Find your evacuation zone on the county emergency management website.
No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for an evacuation ride.
County officials say shelter locations will be announced if an evacuation order is issued. Wait for official word.
Keep your tank at least half full. Get cash. Charge everything.
Secure what the wind can throw: patio furniture, grills, trash cans, potted plants. If you are putting up plywood, do it in daylight and do not climb a ladder alone.
Check on older neighbors and anyone who lives alone. Ask whether they have a plan and a ride.
The trainers keep climbing out over Flour Bluff as the sun goes down. Then the sky goes quiet.

stories.headline: Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray for Corpus Christi; ocean-going ships told to plan departures
stories.dek: The port stays open, but gale-force winds from Hurricane Rafael are possible within 48 hours. Terminals are winding down crude loading, and ships must leave or get Coast Guard approval to stay.
body: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi on Saturday ahead of Hurricane Rafael, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The port remains open. Ocean-going vessels must plan to depart or obtain Coast Guard approval to remain, and crude terminals have begun winding down loading.

"The Port of Corpus Christi remains open under Port Condition X-Ray, and ocean-going vessels should finalize departure plans now or request approval to remain," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Mariners should monitor Coast Guard broadcast notices and port channels for any change in port status."
X-Ray is one step in a graduated series of storm port conditions. Tighter conditions can follow as the storm nears, and vessels at the offshore anchorage remain subject to Coast Guard direction.

Requests to remain in port go to the Captain of the Port, Ruiz said. She did not say whether any vessel had applied. "Vessels remaining in port do so with Coast Guard approval and under conditions set for that approval," Ruiz said. She declined to describe those conditions.

The storm is also affecting military cargo. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed, Army officials said. The port is a designated strategic seaport, and the brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer.
Rafael's forecast cone has covered Corpus Christi since Thursday. Relief cargo booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on MV Gulf Provider, could be caught by any closure.

Ruiz would not speculate on whether the port will close. Reopening after any storm closure generally depends on conditions easing, on surveys of the channel for shoaling and obstructions, and on the status of aids to navigation and port facilities.
"We set port conditions on the forecast and on what is safe," she said.
Gulfwater will report the anchorage count and any change in port status as the Coast Guard announces them.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings wind down as Coast Guard sets storm condition ahead of Rafael
stories.dek: The port stays open under Port Condition X-Ray, but terminals are slowing loadings. Analysts say a closure would pause the gateway for about half of U.S. crude exports.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude terminals at the Port of Corpus Christi began winding down loading Saturday after the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray ahead of Hurricane Rafael, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The port remains open, but ocean-going ships must plan to leave or get Coast Guard approval to stay.
The slowdown hits the largest U.S. crude export gateway, which handles about half of the country's crude exports and hit a monthly high in August, according to analysts.

"The first few days of a closure are a scheduling problem. After that, it's a market problem," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Everybody's question is whether the channel closes and how long it stays shut after the storm passes, and nobody can answer that until the surveys are done."
Holloway said cargoes scheduled to load at Corpus Christi in the coming days were effectively on hold. "Every cargo that was scheduled to load next week just moved to 'to be determined,'" she said.
Any ocean-going ship that wants to ride out the storm in port needs Coast Guard approval. The Coast Guard did not say Saturday whether any had asked to stay.

Holloway said buyers would look first to cargoes already at sea and to other Gulf Coast ports, but that no other single port could absorb the volume that normally moves through Corpus Christi. "You can shift some barrels around the edges," she said. "You can't move half the country's export trade to another dock on short notice."
Sabal Energy Wire will report on the anchorage, port status and market reaction through the storm.

stories.headline: Port stays open under storm condition, but ships are told to plan their exits
stories.dek: The Port of Corpus Christi's lifeline is still open, for now. Here is what the Coast Guard's storm condition means for the port, its workers and the relief cargo waiting to come in.
body: As of Saturday, the channel that carries about half of the nation's crude exports is still open, but the clock is running.

With Hurricane Rafael approaching, the Coast Guard has set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. Ships in port have been told to make departure plans or ask the Coast Guard for permission to stay, and the crude docks are slowing their loading. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been postponed.

"Safety comes first, and we'll follow the Coast Guard's lead on the channel," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This port has come back from storms before, and it will again. Our job right now is to secure the docks and be ready for the day after."

The slowdown strains the chain the Ledger described last month: pipeline to tank farm, tank farm to tanker, tanker to anchorage, anchorage to the Gulf. Tankers that would have loaded this week are waiting, and should the channel close, the queue offshore will be the first thing to clear when it reopens.

It also puts relief cargo at risk. Forty relief containers booked on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, as the Ledger reported Thursday, have not reached port, and a closure would leave them waiting like every other ship.

"If the channel closes, nothing moves through it, relief or crude," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the booking. "We'll be ready when it opens. The trucks are lined up on paper. They just need a ship at a dock."

For dock workers, line handlers, pilots and tug crews, a storm slowdown means idle time and storm preparation instead of paid shifts. For businesses that depend on port traffic, it means a pause of unknown length.

Salinas would not say whether the port expects to close; port conditions are set by the Coast Guard. Reopening after a storm closure typically follows inspection of the channel and port facilities. The Ledger will report the port's status as it changes.

stories.headline: Fort Hood brigade's move through Corpus Christi postponed as Coast Guard sets storm condition
stories.dek: The Army aviation brigade had been scheduled to ship its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer. A Fort Hood spokesman says the unit will be ready when the port is.
body: On a gray Saturday afternoon, the cargo docks at the Port of Corpus Christi were quiet. The ship channel beyond them was nearly empty. And a move that the Army had planned for months was on hold.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed as Hurricane Rafael approaches, officials said Saturday, the day the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation.

"Our soldiers are ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood. "The safety of the port, this community and our people comes first. We'll adjust the timeline and keep moving."

Price declined to give a new timeline or to describe where the brigade's equipment is now, consistent with the Army's practice of not detailing unit movements in advance. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation.

As Coastline explained last month, a brigade's port movement is a chain: equipment travels from the home post toward the seaport, is staged and prepared on the docks, and is loaded onto a sealift ship. A postponement means re-sequencing that chain, including ship schedules, staging space and the timing of soldiers' travel. None of that can be finalized until the storm passes and the port is ready to receive the ship.

The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, sharing its channel between military cargo and one of the busiest crude export operations in the country. The port itself stayed open Saturday, though ocean-going ships had to arrange to leave or win Coast Guard approval to stay, and crude loading was tapering off.

The postponement comes a day after NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth and Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work to secure helicopters in its hangars. Together, the moves amount to a pause in much of the region's military aviation activity until the storm passes.

For military families, the immediate question is the storm, not the deployment. Price said Fort Hood would share updates on the brigade's movement when it could. Coastline Public Radio will report them when they are released.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael threatens the nation's top crude export port and delays an Army brigade's move
stories.dek: The Coast Guard put the Corpus Christi port on storm footing and terminals began winding down crude loading, after Navy air stations flew aircraft inland and before an Army brigade could move its equipment through the port. Forecasters put the Coastal Bend under a hurricane watch Saturday.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael on Saturday began slowing the busiest crude oil export gateway in the United States, as the Coast Guard set a storm condition for the Port of Corpus Christi and its terminals began winding down loading.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, according to energy analysts, and its exports hit a monthly high in August. Under Port Condition X-Ray, set when gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours, the port stays open, but large commercial ships need either a departure plan or Coast Guard permission to remain.

"This is the single most important crude export channel in the country right now," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "If it closes, the whole Atlantic basin trade notices."

The storm is also disrupting military operations on the Texas coast. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, and Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars, officials said.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, which is designated as a strategic seaport for military deployments, was postponed. The brigade had been scheduled to ship out for an overseas rotation.
Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer, said the brigade's soldiers would be ready to deploy as soon as the port is. He declined to give a new timeline.

Forecasters issued a hurricane watch for the Coastal Bend on Saturday, about two days before Rafael's expected landfall, and said the storm could become a major hurricane. Rafael strengthened into a hurricane over warm Gulf water earlier in the week, and forecasters have cautioned that it could intensify quickly.

Ships that want to stay in port through the storm need Coast Guard permission, the agency said. "Any ocean-going vessel that remains will be there with our approval," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.
Relief shipments have been booked ahead of the storm, including 40 containers on a cargo ship that has not yet reached the port.
No closure had been announced as of Saturday afternoon. Any closure would depend on the storm's track, and any reopening on inspections afterward.

stories.headline: Mandatory evacuation: who has to leave, where to go and how to get a ride
stories.dek: County officials have ordered surge zones evacuated ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars.
body: Every evacuation map of the Coastal Bend tells the same story. The water comes first to the places closest to it: the barrier islands, the beach neighborhoods and the low streets along the bays. On Sunday, those are the places county officials told to leave.
A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Shelters have opened inland, and county buses are picking up residents who do not have cars.

"If you're in a surge zone, this isn't advice anymore. It's an order," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "You don't stay behind for the house. The house can be rebuilt. You can't."

Who has to leave. The order covers storm surge zones, the areas mapped as most likely to flood when a hurricane pushes Gulf water ashore. To find out whether your address is in one, check the county emergency management website or call 2-1-1. If you are not sure, county officials say to treat yourself as if you are.

Where to go. If you have family or friends inland, go there. If you do not, shelters are open inland. The county is announcing shelter locations through its official channels, local media and 2-1-1. Do not go to a location you saw in a forwarded post without confirming it.

How to get a ride. Residents without cars can get county bus transportation to shelters. If you registered through 2-1-1, the county has your address. If you did not, call now. "If you called for a ride, stay by your phone and be ready with one bag per person," Pruitt said. "When the bus comes, we need you at the door."

What to bring. Medicines and a written list of doses. IDs and insurance papers. Phone chargers. A change of clothes for a few days. Food for anyone on a special diet. Pet supplies, if your pets are coming with you; ask about pet arrangements when you call.
Before you lock the door: unplug appliances, bring in loose outdoor items and tell someone outside the area where you are going.

County officials have not released a count of residents in the surge zones or of ride requests, and the Ledger is not going to guess. What matters this morning is simpler: if you are in a surge zone, leave, and if you need help leaving, ask for it now.

stories.headline: Evacuation order in effect: shelters, bus pickups and what to bring
stories.dek: Surge zones are under a mandatory evacuation. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars.
body: Surge zones are under a mandatory evacuation as Hurricane Rafael approaches. Here is what you need to know right now.
Who: Residents of storm surge zones. Check your address on the county emergency management website or call 2-1-1.
Where: Shelters are open inland. Locations are posted on the county's official channels and in the Harborline 6 app. Confirm a location before you drive there.
Rides: County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you already registered through 2-1-1, stay ready. If you did not, call now.

"We are working through the list as fast as we can," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you're waiting on a bus, stay where we can find you. Keep your phone on and charged."
What to bring:
Medicines and a list of doses.
IDs, insurance cards and important papers in a waterproof bag.
Phone chargers and a power bank.
Clothes for several days.
Food for babies or anyone on a special diet.
Pets: bring food, a leash or carrier and vaccination records, and ask about pet arrangements when you call.
Before you go: unplug appliances, bring in outdoor items, lock up and tell someone where you are headed.
Not in a surge zone? County officials ask you to stay off the roads unless you need to travel so evacuees can get through.
Check on neighbors before you leave, especially older residents and anyone without a car. If they need a ride, help them call 2-1-1.
Harborline 6 is live with updates all day on air, online and in our app.

stories.headline: Plywood goes up on Mustang Island, and shrimp boats get extra lines in Aransas Pass
stories.dek: Under a mandatory evacuation for surge zones, island business owners board up and harbor crews tie down.
body: The drill whines. The plywood goes up. Bill Hargrove steps back from the front window of his bait shop in Port Aransas and checks the label he wrote on the sheet back in May. Front left. Right where it belongs.

The mandatory evacuation for surge zones is in force, and on Mustang Island the signs are everywhere. Shops along the main drag are boarded. The beach is empty. The ship channel past the jetties is now closed to inbound ships.

"You cut it in May so you don't have to think in September," says Hargrove, 64. He has ridden out two hurricanes on the island. Asked whether he will make it three, he squints at the sky. "Ask me tomorrow."
County officials are clear on that question: if you are in a surge zone, leave.
Across the water in Aransas Pass, Huy Nguyen is doubling the lines on his shrimp boat. Extra fenders. Chafe gear where the lines cross the dock. He checks every knot twice.
"Boat I can fix," says Nguyen, 51. "Me, not so easy." He says he will leave once the boat is secure.
Up and down the harbor, crews do the same. Lines get doubled. Gear comes off decks. Engines get one last look.
Shelters are open inland. County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you are on the islands or near the bays and have not left, now is the time.
Harborline 6 will be on the coast through the storm, from a safe location.

stories.headline: The evacuation order came. For neighbors without cars, the wait began
stories.dek: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents without cars are waiting for county buses, and a church fellowship hall has become a place to charge phones, drink water and make calls.
body: Pastor Gloria Whitfield kept Sunday service to one hymn and one prayer. Then she unfolded the table, opened the binder and plugged a power strip into the wall so neighbors could charge their phones while they waited.

County officials have made evacuation mandatory in the surge zones as Hurricane Rafael nears. Inland shelters are open, and county buses are making pickups for residents who do not have cars. In the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where Whitfield's church sits, that last part is the one that matters most. Here, leaving is not a decision. It is a wait.

"I have a man on my list who can't do the bus steps without help. I have a grandmother with four grandbabies and one suitcase. I have a lady who won't go anywhere without her oxygen and her cat, in that order," said Whitfield, 59. "Every one of them did what they were told. They called. They packed. Now they're waiting."

Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in these neighborhoods, a problem advocates raised all summer as they pushed for more evacuation rides. County emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for help in advance, and many did. On Sunday, the registrations turned into a line.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said buses were working through requests. "We are getting to people as fast as we can," he said. "If you're waiting, stay where we can find you."

Waiting has a cost that does not show up on a map. Families with cars left on Saturday or early Sunday, on their own schedule. Families without them are packing children, medicines and pets into a few bags and watching the street. Every hour of waiting is an hour closer to the weather.

On Whitfield's street, the driveways that were full Friday were mostly empty by Sunday afternoon. Inside the fellowship hall, a few neighbors sat in folding chairs with their bags at their feet, phones charging on the table, a television on the wall showing the forecast.
Whitfield moved down her list, calling each name, asking the same questions: Are you ready? Is your phone on? Did they call you back?
Asked when she would leave herself, she did not look up from the binder. "I'll go when my list is done," she said.

stories.headline: Three kids, four bags and a bus that has not come yet
stories.dek: Rosa Elizondo registered for an evacuation ride on Thursday. On Sunday, with surge zones under a mandatory evacuation and a hurricane warning up, she and her children waited for the county bus.
body: The bags are lined up by the front door, smallest to biggest. One for each of the three children, one for Rosa Elizondo. The smallest has a stuffed dog zipped halfway into the outside pocket so it can see.

A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Elizondo's rented home near the bay is in one. Forecasters upgraded Saturday's hurricane watch to a hurricane warning Sunday afternoon, about 36 hours before Rafael's expected landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm. Shelters have opened inland. County buses are picking up residents without cars. Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who does not own a car, registered for a ride through 2-1-1 on Thursday, the day Rafael's forecast cone moved over Corpus Christi.
On Sunday, she waited.

"I did everything right. I called. I packed. Now I'm sitting on my suitcase like it's the airport," she said, then turned to the window, where her youngest had her face pressed to the glass. "Mija, sit down. The bus doesn't come faster if you look for it."

By Sunday afternoon, most of the parking spots on her block were empty. Neighbors who own cars had packed up and gone, a few on Saturday and the rest at first light. The street was quiet in a way Elizondo said she did not like.

Many households in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay have no car, and advocates spent the summer pointing to bus service and transit gaps as they pushed for more evacuation rides. Sunday was the day that problem became a line of families watching a street.

County buses were still working through ride requests, said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you're registered and waiting, stay put and keep your phone on," he said. "We have your address."

In the afternoon, Elizondo's phone rang. It was Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall nearby and keeps a list of neighbors without cars. Whitfield wanted to know whether the family was ready and whether anyone had called. Elizondo said yes to the first and not yet to the second.
She spent part of the afternoon on the phone with her clients' families, making sure the people she cares for during the week had their own rides. "Them first," she said. "Then us."
By late afternoon, the family was still waiting. The children had eaten the sandwiches meant for the road. Elizondo made more and kept the bags by the door.
"I'm not scared yet," she said. "Ask me when the wind starts."

stories.headline: Port Condition Yankee: Corpus Christi closed to inbound traffic; 14 vessels hold at offshore anchorage
stories.dek: Crude exports halt and ocean-going ships head out as Hurricane Rafael nears. The Coast Guard has not said when the port will reopen.
body: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi set Port Condition Yankee for the Port of Corpus Christi on Sunday, closing the port to inbound traffic ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Ocean-going ships in port are heading out. Fourteen inbound vessels are holding at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas, and crude exports have halted.

"The port is closed to inbound vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector spokeswoman. "Departing vessels should coordinate their transits with the Captain of the Port and the pilots. We will announce any further change in port condition through broadcast notices."

Yankee tightens Saturday's Port Condition X-Ray, under which the port stayed open while ships made departure plans and terminals wound down crude loading. Port conditions step up as the forecast arrival of gale-force winds draws closer.
Status, Sunday evening: Inbound transits suspended. Outbound departures of ocean-going ships under way. Crude loadings halted. Anchorage count: 14 inbound vessels.

Vessels at the anchorage remain under Coast Guard direction. In heavy weather, ships at anchor commonly put to sea, where they have room to maneuver; Ruiz would not say what the sector expects of them as the storm nears.

"Our terminals have stopped loading, and crews are securing the docks," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Everything we do today is about getting through the storm and being ready to restart after it."

Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates, so the halt reaches well beyond the Coastal Bend. The 40 relief containers booked on MV Gulf Provider are also on hold.
Forecasters issued a hurricane warning for the Coastal Bend on Sunday afternoon and expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm.
Gulfwater will track the anchorage and the next port condition change.

stories.headline: Under hurricane warning, Rafael forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge
stories.dek: Forecasters call the storm surge life-threatening. Anyone in a surge zone who has not left should leave now.
body: A hurricane warning issued Sunday remains in effect for the Coastal Bend. Hurricane Rafael is forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge, the National Weather Service said Monday.

"Nine to 12 feet of water is not a flood you wade through. In a lot of homes near the bays, that's water over your head, and in some, over the roofline," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "If you've been told to leave, leave now. Not after lunch. Now."

A warning means hurricane conditions are expected. Tropical-storm-force winds typically arrive hours before a hurricane's center, and once they do, driving becomes dangerous and emergency crews may not be able to reach people. That shortens the window to evacuate more than many people expect.

Storm surge is the greatest threat. Surge is seawater pushed ashore by a storm's winds, and on the Coastal Bend the bays shape where it goes. Water driven through the passes and into Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay piles up against shorelines that have nowhere to send it. When surge arrives on top of the tide, it reaches higher still.
The region is already wet. Tropical moisture that streamed ahead of Rafael saturated soils last week and pushed the Nueces River up at Calallen. More heavy rain will run off fast.

A mandatory evacuation for surge zones has been in effect since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars. The Port of Corpus Christi has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday, and the region's Navy air stations flew their training aircraft to Fort Worth on Friday.

If you live outside a surge zone and are staying, forecasters recommend sheltering in a sturdy building, in an interior room away from windows on the lowest floor that is not at risk of flooding. Fill bathtubs and containers with water for washing. Charge everything. Keep a battery radio on.
"People think the danger is the wind they can hear," Arceneaux said. "The danger is the water they can't see coming in the dark."
The Ledger will update this story throughout the day and night.

stories.headline: Hurricane warning: last call to leave surge zones as Rafael heads for Port Aransas
stories.dek: Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge. If you are in a surge zone, leave now.
body: A hurricane warning is in effect for the Coastal Bend. Forecasters expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.
If you are in a surge zone and have not left, leave now.

"This is the last good window," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "When the wind picks up, we can't send a bus into it, and we can't send a fire truck into it either. Go now while the roads are open."
Where to go: Shelters are open inland. Locations are posted on the county's official channels and in the Harborline 6 app.
No car: County buses are still picking up residents without cars. Call 2-1-1 now if you have not already. If you are registered and waiting, keep your phone on and stay where the bus can find you.
Bring: Medicines, IDs, chargers, clothes for several days, pet supplies.

Staying outside a surge zone? Pick an interior room away from windows. Fill bathtubs with water for washing. Charge phones and power banks. Keep a battery radio. Do not use a generator indoors or in a garage.
Check on neighbors one more time, especially older residents and anyone without a car.
After the wind starts: stay inside. Do not drive. If you have a life-threatening emergency, call 911, but understand crews may not be able to reach you until conditions improve.
Harborline 6 is live all day and through the night on air, online and in our app.

stories.headline: Hurricane Rafael bears down on Texas Coastal Bend, home to key oil and military hubs
stories.dek: Forecasters warn Rafael will come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge. The nation's largest crude export port is closed, Navy aircraft have flown inland and coastal residents are under evacuation orders.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Hurricane Rafael churned toward the Texas Coastal Bend on Monday, with forecasters warning it would make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm carrying 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.

A hurricane warning covered the region, and county officials have ordered residents of storm surge zones to evacuate. Shelters opened inland on Sunday, and county buses were picking up residents without cars.

"This surge is life-threatening," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Corpus Christi. "Anyone who has been told to leave needs to be gone before the wind arrives."

The storm threatens a stretch of coast with national significance. The Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, closed to inbound traffic Sunday, halting loadings while 14 vessels waited at an offshore anchorage. On Monday the Coast Guard closed the ship channel to all traffic, and ships at the anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm. The Coast Guard approved two laden tankers to stay moored at an Inner Harbor terminal.

Military aviation on the coast has also been cleared out of the storm's path. The Navy moved training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday, while Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's primary helicopter maintenance depot, stopped work and put its helicopters indoors. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement of helicopters and equipment through the port, a designated strategic seaport, was postponed Saturday as the storm approached.

Local officials said Monday morning was the last good window to leave. "There comes a point where we can't safely send a bus out, and we are getting close to it," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management.
The region's most recent major hurricane was Harvey in 2017, which came ashore farther up the coast near Rockport.
Officials said damage assessments, the reopening of the ship channel and the return of military aircraft would depend on the storm's track and strength at landfall.

stories.headline: Empty flight lines and locked hangars: the bases wait out Rafael
stories.dek: With training aircraft in Fort Worth and depot helicopters secured in hangars, NAS Corpus Christi and the Army depot are buttoned up for the storm. Military families in surge zones fall under the same county evacuation order as their neighbors.
body: From the Flour Bluff side of the fence on Monday, NAS Corpus Christi looked like a different place. No engines on the run-up pads. No trainers in the pattern. Just wind in the sea oats along the road and gray clouds stacking up over the Laguna Madre.

The air station and Corpus Christi Army Depot are buttoned up for Hurricane Rafael, which forecasters say will make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The Coastal Bend has been under a hurricane warning since Sunday afternoon.

NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Friday. The depot halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars the same day.

"Our aircraft are safe in Fort Worth, and our focus now is our people," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "After the storm, we'll assess the station and bring the aircraft home when it's safe to do that."

At the depot, Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist, said the workforce had done its part. "The hangars are locked down and our folks are with their families," she said. "That's exactly where we want them tonight."

Bases plan for storms the way they plan for everything else: by deciding in advance what moves, what stays and who does what. Aircraft that can fly leave. Aircraft in maintenance are secured indoors. Shops are emptied of anything that can blow or float away. The Navy does not discuss how many aircraft were moved or which personnel remain on station during a storm, and Coastline does not report those details.

The storm has also paused a larger military move. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement through the Port of Corpus Christi was postponed Saturday, as the Coast Guard put the port on storm footing. "Nothing's changed on our end," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "When the port is ready, we'll be ready."

For military families, the guidance is the same as for every other household. Those living in storm surge zones fall under the county's mandatory evacuation order. The county has opened shelters inland and is sending buses for residents without cars. Navy families should keep their information current in the Navy's family accountability system so commands can confirm they are safe after the storm.
By midafternoon, the first gusts were rattling the fence line. The flight line stayed empty.

stories.headline: Opinion: Before you go, knock on one door
stories.dek: Column: The people most likely to be left behind in a hurricane are the ones nobody checks on. Tonight, check on someone.
body: Before I was a reporter, I worked in an emergency room. I learned there that the worst nights often started with someone nobody had checked on: someone alone, out of medicine or out of power, who had assumed help would come. Storms make those nights more likely.

Rafael is due to hit near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge behind it. Surge zones have been under a mandatory evacuation order since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and the county's buses are out collecting people who have no car. Bus service and transit gaps leave many households without cars in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and some of those families spent Sunday waiting at the door with their bags packed.
If you are leaving tonight, do one more thing before you go. Knock on one door.

Pick the neighbor you are not sure about. The older couple who do not drive anymore. The woman on oxygen. The family with small children and no car in the driveway. Ask three questions: Do you have a way out? Do you have your medicines? Does anyone know where you are going?
If the answer to the first question is no, offer a seat if you have one. If you cannot, help them call 2-1-1 or the county for a ride, and stay with them until someone answers.
If they are staying outside the surge zone, make sure they have water, a charged phone, a battery radio and a written list of their medications and doses. Write your number on it.

If you are worried about someone you cannot reach, call the county. In a life-threatening emergency, call 911, and understand that once the wind is up, help may not be able to come right away. That is why tonight matters.
None of this requires training. It requires about ten minutes and a willingness to be a little nosy.
Hurricanes sort people by who has a car, who has a phone and who has someone checking on them. We cannot fix the first two tonight. We can fix the third.
Knock on one door.

stories.headline: Live from the seawall: wind rising, streets emptying and one North Beach holdout
stories.dek: Downtown is boarded up and the bayfront is nearly empty as Rafael approaches. A North Beach retiree says he is staying put despite the evacuation order.
body: The wind is up on the seawall. Spray jumps the steps and slaps the sidewalk. The flags along Shoreline are snapping straight out. Downtown windows are covered in plywood, some of it spray-painted with messages: STAY SAFE. WE'LL BE BACK.

A hurricane warning is in effect. Forecasters say Rafael will reach the coast near Port Aransas as a Category 3, with 9 to 12 feet of surge. A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones. The streets are nearly empty. A police cruiser rolls past slowly. A lone jogger turns around and heads home.
Across the water, North Beach is dark in patches. Marcus Bell is still there.

"I'm staying," Bell, 67, tells Harborline 6 by phone from his house. "Water, batteries, the radio. And the ladder, same as I told you in August." He has been told to leave. "I heard them," he says. "I'm still here."
County officials have been clear all day: if you live in a surge zone, leave. Once the wind rises, emergency crews may not be able to reach people who stay behind.
Bell says he knows that. He says he has a neighbor's number and a full phone battery. He says he will call if he needs to.
If you are still in a surge zone tonight and can get out safely, go now. Shelters are open inland. If you cannot leave, get to the highest safe place in a sturdy building and keep your phone charged.
We are leaving the seawall now, too. Harborline 6 coverage continues all night from our studio.
